content: 1. Nasopharyngeal aspirates, gastric aspirates, and stool samples are preferred over smear microscopy, culture, and phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (DST) for diagnosing tuberculosis (TB). This recommendation is strong for sputum testing due to moderate certainty of evidence for accuracy, but evidence for accuracy in gastric aspirates, nasopharyngeal aspirates, and stool samples is of low certainty. 2. In adults presenting with symptoms of pulmonary TB and no history of TB treatment within the last five years, or with a remote history of TB treatment (more than five years ago), the Xpert Ultra test should be used as the initial diagnostic tool for TB and rifampicin resistance detection in sputum. This is strongly recommended with high certainty of evidence for test accuracy. 3. In adults with symptoms of pulmonary TB and a history of TB treatment completed within the last five years, Xpert Ultra may be used as the initial diagnostic test for TB and rifampicin resistance detection in sputum. This is a conditional recommendation with low certainty of evidence for test accuracy. 4. In children with symptoms of pulmonary TB, Xpert Ultra should be used as the initial diagnostic test for TB and rifampicin resistance detection in sputum or nasopharyngeal aspirates. This is strongly recommended, but the certainty of evidence for test accuracy is low for sputum and very low for nasopharyngeal aspirates. 5. For adults and children with symptoms of TB meningitis, Xpert MTB/RIF or Xpert Ultra should be used on cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) as the initial diagnostic test rather than smear microscopy or culture. This is strongly recommended, with moderate certainty of evidence for Xpert MTB/RIF and low certainty for Xpert Ultra. 6. In adults and children with symptoms of extrapulmonary TB, Xpert MTB/RIF may be used on lymph node aspirates, lymph node biopsies, pleural fluid, peritoneal fluid, pericardial fluid, synovial fluid, or urine as the initial diagnostic test for the respective forms of extrapulmonary TB. This is a conditional recommendation with varying levels of evidence certainty: moderate for pleural fluid, low for lymph node aspirates, peritoneal fluid, synovial fluid, and urine, and very low for pericardial fluid and lymph node biopsies. 7. In adults and children with symptoms of extrapulmonary TB, Xpert Ultra may be used on lymph node aspirates and biopsies as the initial diagnostic test for lymph node TB. This is a conditional recommendation with low certainty of evidence. 8. For adults and children with symptoms of extrapulmonary TB, Xpert MTB/RIF or Xpert Ultra should be used for rifampicin resistance detection rather than culture and phenotypic DST. This is strongly recommended, with high certainty of evidence for Xpert MTB/RIF and low certainty for Xpert Ultra. 9. In HIV-positive adults and children with symptoms of disseminated TB, Xpert MTB/RIF may be used on blood as an initial diagnostic test for disseminated TB. This is a conditional recommendation with very low certainty of evidence for test accuracy. 10. In adults with symptoms of pulmonary TB who have an Xpert Ultra trace-positive result on the initial test, repeated testing with Xpert Ultra may not be necessary. This is a conditional recommendation with very low certainty of evidence for test accuracy. 11. In children with symptoms of pulmonary TB in settings with a pretest probability below 5% and a negative Xpert MTB/RIF result on the initial test, repeated testing with Xpert MTB/RIF on sputum, gastric fluid, nasopharyngeal aspirates, or stool specimens may not be necessary. This is a conditional recommendation with low certainty of evidence for sputum and very low certainty for other specimen types. 12. In children with symptoms of pulmonary TB in settings with a pretest probability of 5% or more and a negative Xpert MTB/RIF result on the initial test, a second Xpert MTB/RIF test (for a total of two tests) on sputum, gastric fluid, nasopharyngeal aspirates, or stool specimens may be used. This is a conditional recommendation with low certainty of evidence for sputum and very low certainty for other specimen types. 13. In children with symptoms of pulmonary TB in settings with a pretest probability below 5% and a negative Xpert Ultra result on the initial test, repeated testing with Xpert Ultra on sputum or nasopharyngeal aspirates may not be necessary. This is a conditional recommendation with very low certainty of evidence for test accuracy. 14. In children with symptoms of pulmonary TB in settings with a pretest probability of 5% or more and a negative Xpert Ultra result on the first test, a second Xpert Ultra test (for a total of two tests) on sputum and nasopharyngeal aspirates may be used. This is a conditional recommendation with very low certainty of evidence for test accuracy. 15. In adults in the general population with either symptoms of TB, chest radiograph abnormalities, or both, Xpert MTB/RIF or Xpert Ultra may replace culture as the initial test for pulmonary TB. This is a conditional recommendation with low certainty of evidence for Xpert MTB/RIF and moderate certainty for Xpert Ultra. 16. In adults in the general population with a positive TB symptom screen, chest radiograph abnormalities, or both, a single Xpert Ultra test may be used as the initial test for pulmonary TB rather than two Xpert Ultra tests. This is a conditional recommendation with very low certainty of evidence for test accuracy. 17. In adults and children with symptoms of pulmonary TB, the Truenat MTB or MTB Plus test may be used as an initial diagnostic test for TB rather than smear microscopy or culture. This is a conditional recommendation with moderate certainty of evidence for test accuracy. 18. In adults and children with symptoms of pulmonary TB and a positive Truenat MTB or MTB Plus result, the Truenat MTB-RIF Dx test may be used as an initial test for rifampicin resistance rather than culture and phenotypic DST. This is a conditional recommendation with very low certainty of evidence for test accuracy. 19. Chest radiography is a valuable tool for diagnosing childhood TB, particularly when combined with clinical and exposure history, evidence of TB infection, and microbiological testing. Posteroanterior (PA) and lateral chest radiograph views should be obtained if possible. Abnormal findings on chest radiography warrant a full diagnostic evaluation. 20. Chest radiography can improve the efficiency of using the Xpert MTB/RIF assay by helping to triage individuals for testing, reducing the number of tests and associated costs, and improving the pretest probability for TB, thereby enhancing the predictive value of the assay. 21. Chest radiography is particularly useful in diagnosing TB among people living with HIV, especially for ruling out TB disease before initiating treatment for latent TB infection. 22. All individuals diagnosed with TB should receive effective treatment and support tailored to their needs to ensure adherence. This includes addressing basic needs such as food, water, and housing, especially in emergency settings. 23. TB treatment regimens involve a combination of drugs taken daily over several months. The intensive phase includes multiple drugs to rapidly kill the bacteria, followed by a continuation phase with fewer drugs to eliminate any remaining bacteria. 24. Drug-resistant TB arises from genetic mutations in Mycobacterium tuberculosis, either due to inadequate treatment (secondary resistance) or transmission of resistant strains (primary resistance). 25. First-line TB treatment for drug-susceptible TB involves highly effective, all-oral drugs in standardized regimens, regardless of bacteriological or HIV status. Fixed-dose combinations (FDCs) are recommended to simplify treatment and improve adherence. 26. Patient-centered care and support are essential to maximize treatment adherence and detect non-responders early. This approach should be introduced as soon as possible, even in humanitarian emergencies. 27. All TB patients should be regularly monitored to assess their response to therapy, identify adverse drug effects, and manage comorbidities. A written record of medications, bacteriological response, and adverse effects should be maintained for each patient. 28. Adverse drug reactions should be promptly detected and managed, sometimes requiring hospitalization. Patients should be educated on recognizing and reporting common side effects. 29. Active TB drug safety monitoring and management (aDSM) involves systematic clinical and laboratory assessments to detect serious adverse events in patients on second-line TB drugs. This data should be reported to national pharmacovigilance authorities.
